extracted.intended_audience: readers of Mark Twain letters / general literary readers and scholars
extracted.subtask_description: A set of evaluative questions and expectations (posed by Mark Twain) for judging the literary quality of novels, and related normative expectations about prose, recommendation letters, telegraphic service, and attitudes toward originality/plagiarism, as found in his letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages in good English
rubrics_metrics.description: 1. Are there in Sir Walter's novels passages done in good English--English which is neither slovenly or involved?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Twain asks whether Scott ever writes English that is clean and properly constructed rather than careless or overwrought; this is used as a primary test of literary competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages above commonplace quality
rubrics_metrics.description: 2. Are there passages whose English is not poor and thin and commonplace, but is of a quality above that?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeks instances of language that rises above banality — not merely competent but noticeably elevated in quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passages that 'burn with real fire'
rubrics_metrics.description: 3. Are there passages which burn with real fire--not punk, fox-fire, make believe?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looks for genuine passion or intensity in prose, as opposed to artificial or merely pretended emotional effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorable heroes and heroines
rubrics_metrics.description: 4. Has he heroes and heroines who are not cads and cadesses?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates moral and sympathetic credibility of protagonists; asks whether lead characters possess integrity rather than being contemptible or shallow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character and action
rubrics_metrics.description: 5. Has he personages whose acts and talk correspond with their characters as described by him?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checks whether characters behave and speak in ways consistent with their established traits — internal logic and verisimilitude of characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admirable protagonists with clear reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: 6. Has he heroes and heroines whom the reader admires, admires, and knows why?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not only must protagonists be admirable, but the text should make clear the grounds for that admiration; the reader should understand and share the admiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic humor and humorous characters
rubrics_metrics.description: 7. Has he funny characters that are funny, and humorous passages that are humorous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assesses whether comedic elements genuinely amuse and whether comic characters are truly comic rather than forced or artificial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to sustain reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: 8. Does he ever chain the reader's interest, and make him reluctant to lay the book down?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A work's capacity to engross the reader — pacing, suspense, and engagement that compel continued reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity vs posing
rubrics_metrics.description: 9. Are there pages where he ceases from posing, ceases from admiring the placid flood and flow of his own dilutions, ceases from being artificial, and is for a time, long or short, recognizably sincere and in earnest?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Looks for moments of genuine sincerity and earnestness amid otherwise artificial or performative writing; values authenticity of voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of English but failure to use it
rubrics_metrics.description: 10. Did he know how to write English, and didn't do it because he didn't want to?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions whether poor prose results from inability or from choice; implies a different critique if the author can write well but prefers not to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice competence
rubrics_metrics.description: 11. Did he use the right word only when he couldn't think of another one, or did he run so much to wrong because he didn't know the right one when he saw it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between occasional lapses and systematic ignorance of vocabulary; assesses author's command of diction and precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall maintainable respect
rubrics_metrics.description: 13. Can you read him? and keep your respect for him? Of course a person could in his day--an era of sentimentality and sloppy romantics--but land! can a body do it today?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A global litmus test: whether the reader can continue reading the author while retaining respect; tied to changing standards and historical context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prose quality in scholarly/translation work
rubrics_metrics.description: Grace, beauty and limpidity of English prose in a scholarly translation or monograph (e.g., 'the grace and beauty and limpidity of the book's unsurpassable English').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Twain praises Goodman's Mayan translation for clarity, elegance, erudition and readable English — indicating that scientific/antiquarian writing should aim for lucid, graceful, and dignified prose, not obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphic service: timeliness and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Telegraphic service should be prompt, should not forward messages known to be worthless, and should provide transparent timing information on dispatch/receipt (criticized blank: no field for start time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From Clemens's complaint: a competent telegraph service must deliver messages in time to be useful, provide records/timestamps so recipients can judge delays, avoid charging for transport that renders a message worthless, and ensure operational staff exercise judgment rather than blind adherence to rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of a credible recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: What to include in a public recommendation: mention of the candidate's experience, authoritative endorsements (e.g., a royal letter), candor about the recommender's direct knowledge ('I have had no opportunity to test the validity... but that judgment is the utterance of an entirely competent authority').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemens's recommendation of Madame Hartwig shows that a strong endorsement cites reputable external certification, summarizes relevant experience, and includes honest disclosure about the recommender's personal testing/knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward originality and plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that 'ninety-nine parts of all things that proceed from the intellect are plagiarisms, pure and simple' and that the kernel of utterances is second-hand; the implied standard is modesty about originality and skepticism of harsh treatment of minor imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark Twain argues that most ideas and phrasing are recycled and that accusations of plagiarism can be overblown; the evaluative stance encourages humility about claims of originality and cautions against punitive responses to the common phenomenon of intellectual indebtedness.
